clue.text: A teacher is Piggy's victim

definitions.note: a joking way to name the youth killed by a wild boar

parts.note: taken as written
a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher bullied by a character called Piggy, as if from a school story.
explanation.walkthrough: Piggy suggests Lord of the Flies or Miss Piggy, but here it is a boar: in Greek myth Adonis was gored to death by one.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth the beautiful youth Adonis died from the tusks of a wild boar while out hunting.

clue.text: Help I'd arranged in a sacred place

indicators.note: letters that are arranged are put into a new order, so the clue's own words are reshuffled

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: Someone says they set things out to help in a holy spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Delphi, home of Apollo's oracle, was the most famous holy site of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Probable virgin, a father in the Bible

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a member of a religious order sworn to chastity, so presumably a virgin
second meaning: the father of Joshua in the Old Testament

explanation.walkthrough: Joshua is repeatedly called 'the son of Nun' in the Bible, so the second sense is a man's name, not a religious sister.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman in holy orders takes a vow of chastity, while Joshua's father bears the same name.

clue.text: A lexicographer and a famous poet, cycling

indicators.note: cycling sends letters round from one end of the poet's name to the other, like a wheel turning

parts.note: John Keats, the Romantic poet

explanation.surface: Two literary men, a dictionary-maker and a poet, out on bicycles together.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving the last letter of the poet's name to the front gives the dictionary-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter William Skeat was a Victorian scholar who compiled an etymological dictionary of English.

clue.text: Taste old gin cocktail — it's a Buenos Aires tradition

definitions.note: the gerund names an activity, so 'it' is the dancing itself

parts.note: a tang is a sharp taste

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters of the spirit are mixed up

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A drinker samples an old gin cocktail, said to be customary in Argentina's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancing the tango is the signature custom of Buenos Aires, where the dance was born in the late nineteenth century.

clue.text: Two male brutes meeting bachelor one of John Willet's three cronies

definitions.text: one of John Willet's three cronies

parts.note: a tom is a male cat and a cob a male swan, two male animals

explanation.surface: Two hulking men meet an unmarried man who is a pal of a Dickens innkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: John Willet keeps the Maypole inn in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge; his regular cronies are Tom Cobb, Phil Parkes and Solomon Daisy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Cobb, the chandler and post-office keeper, drinks with landlord John Willet at the Maypole in Barnaby Rudge.

clue.text: One like Cicero, with no volume, Italian chap embracing silence

parts.note: taken as written, the little word no

indicators.note: one word embracing another holds it inside, so the call for quiet goes within the Italian word

parts.note: uomo is Italian for man
sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: An orator like Cicero, without a loud voice, as an Italian man holds his tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no volume' reads as 'quiet' but gives NO plus V; the Latin phrase means 'new man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero was the classic novus homo, a Roman who reached the consulship though none of his ancestors had held office.

clue.text: Somehow one respects this Munro short story collection

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come in some other order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A reader says this Alice Munro book is admired, in some way.
explanation.definitionFit: Open Secrets is Alice Munro's 1994 book of short stories, set largely in small-town Ontario.

clue.text: Not supplied by the military? It doesn't matter

definitions.meaning: first meaning, jokey: something that is not standard issue, as kit is issued by the army
second meaning: a topic of no importance

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical reading: an item the army never issued would be a non-issue.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-issue is a matter of no real importance, something not worth arguing about.

clue.text: Bin helmet nearly destroyed in battle

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

indicators.note: nearly the word means all but its final letter

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter before it is shortened

explanation.surface: Throw your wrecked helmet away, it was nearly destroyed in the fighting.
explanation.definitionFit: Blenheim was Marlborough's great 1704 victory over the French and Bavarians in the War of the Spanish Succession.

clue.text: European destination of an imagined English queen travelling west

indicators.note: in an across clue, travelling west means reading from right to left

parts.note: there has only been one Queen Anne, so a fourth would be invented

explanation.surface: A make-believe English queen heading west towards somewhere in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Vienna, capital of Austria, is a European city people travel to.

clue.text: Article on an English detective fiction character is a famous author's abandoned work

indicators.note: in an across clue the article sits on, that is before, the next piece

parts.note: the definite article
Dr Watson, Sherlock Holmes's companion
the short form of 'is', as in he's

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on Holmes's sidekick turns out to be a lost work by a great writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Detective fiction points to an unfinished mystery, but the author is Jane Austen, who left The Watsons incomplete.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen began The Watsons around 1803 and gave it up, leaving the novel unfinished.

clue.text: Wouk's navy ensign shortly is going to lie with a comedy actress

indicators.note: said shortly, the word loses its last letter

parts.note: will expresses the future
taken as written
Penelope Keith, star of The Good Life and To the Manor Born

explanation.surface: A sailor in a novel will soon lie beside a funny actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' looks like 'soon' but trims the word for the future tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Willie Keith is the young ensign who narrates much of Herman Wouk's naval novel The Caine Mutiny.

clue.text: Without harm in the end, break part of a window

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is left out

parts.note: to smash is to break

indicators.note: in the end picks only the final letter of the word harm

parts.note: the word whose last letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: Someone breaks a pane at last but nobody gets hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is the sliding frame holding the glass in a sash window.

clue.text: 1940s alleged communist organisation abandoned reserve weapon

parts.note: left behind means abandoned
to book is to reserve
a club is a heavy stick used as a weapon

explanation.surface: A shady political group has dropped its spare arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Gollancz's Left Book Club was a left-wing book society, accused of being a Communist front.

clue.text: Meet some characters — some of them appear in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

definitions.text: some of them appear in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
definitions.note: a plural definition for a plural answer

parts.note: to face is to meet head on
a card is an eccentric or amusing person, a real character

explanation.surface: Come and meet the odd folk in Lewis Carroll's book.
explanation.definitionFit: The King, Queen and Knave of Hearts in Carroll's story are court cards from a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: Portrait in oils a man damaged

indicators.note: a damaged thing is out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: An oil painting of a man that has been spoiled.
explanation.walkthrough: The man in the surface is a red herring: the sitter is a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo's Mona Lisa is the world's most famous painted likeness of a sitter.

clue.text: "Come nice thing, let my heart alone, / I cannot live without thee!" (—— , Michael Drayton)

definitions.text: "Come nice thing, let my heart alone, / I cannot live without thee!"
definitions.meaning: the closing lines of a short love poem quoted as a lover's plea
the Elizabethan poet who wrote it, so the blank wants his poem's title

explanation.walkthrough: This is a literary-knowledge clue: the solver supplies the title of the Drayton poem these lines end.
explanation.definitionFit: Drayton's lyric addressed to a shy, teasing sweetheart ends with exactly these lines.

clue.text: Lord's experiences with white rose monarchs

definitions.note: Lord's is the London cricket ground, where batsmen face these balls

parts.note: the white rose was the emblem of the House of York
ER is a monarch's royal cipher, so ERS is the plural

explanation.surface: A nobleman's life among the Yorkist kings.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's looks like a peer but is the London cricket ground; a yorker is a ball pitched right at the batsman's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Batsmen at the home of cricket regularly face full-length deliveries aimed at their toes.

clue.text: Is Indian able to be a king of England?

parts.note: can means is able
the Ute are a Native American people

explanation.surface: Could a Native American ever be crowned in England?
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a question, 'Is Indian able?' becomes 'Can Ute?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Canute, the Danish ruler also called Cnut, reigned as King of England from 1016 to 1035.

clue.text: McEwan's teenage narrator, a sailor and detective

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the adolescent who tells The Cement Garden
second meaning: ..., short for ... tar, is a seaman
third meaning: old slang for a police detective

explanation.walkthrough: Three senses of one name: Ian McEwan's first novel is narrated by the boy Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: The same short name serves for McEwan's boy narrator, a seaman and a plain-clothes policeman.

clue.text: Children's novel with bears, mostly friendly

parts.note: to bear is to carry

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: warm means friendly

explanation.surface: A kids' book about bears that is fairly cosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' suggests animals in the story, but it is a verb meaning carries.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrie's War is Nina Bawden's 1973 book for young readers about evacuees in wartime Wales.

clue.text: Johnsonian philosopher with expensive computer about one pound

indicators.note: about means around, so the computer surrounds the other piece

parts.note: an iMac is Apple's pricey desktop
L is the sign for a pound, from libra

explanation.surface: A sage from Johnson's circle with a costly computer, worth about a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Imlac is the wise poet and philosopher who guides the prince in Samuel Johnson's Rasselas.

clue.text: Turkish minister is reportedly in fight with king

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to vie is to compete or contend

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken, so the word is written as it sounds

parts.note: the word is, said aloud, has a buzzing z sound and is written as it is heard

explanation.surface: An Ottoman minister is said to be in a struggle with the sultan.
explanation.definitionFit: A vizier was a high official, a minister of state, in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: European with charm who helps someone find their desired valentine

definitions.text: who helps someone find their desired valentine

parts.note: glamour is alluring charm

explanation.surface: A charming Continental matchmaker who brings lovers together on Valentine's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: Valentine is not the day of romance but the hero of Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona; Sir Eglamour helps Silvia run off to find him.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's comedy the knight Sir Eglamour escorts Silvia as she flees Milan in search of her beloved.

clue.text: Deface Proust? Not half

indicators.note: not half means only one half survives, so the back three letters go

parts.note: Marcel Proust, the French novelist

explanation.surface: Vandalise a great French novelist? Not a bit of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' also sounds like British slang for 'very much'; here it halves the novelist's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil or disfigure it.

clue.text: Fate of a relative, after long sorrow

indicators.note: after places the relative behind the sorrow

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for long, as in longitude
an ache is a lasting pain or grief
sis, short for sister

explanation.surface: What happened to a family member after a long time of grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fate' reads as destiny but is one of the three Fates of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Lachesis is one of the three Moirai, the goddess who measures out the thread of each life.

clue.text: Gravy maker's one helping to serve beef

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Raymond ..., the American writer whose poem is titled Gravy
second meaning: someone who slices the joint at table

explanation.walkthrough: Gravy sounds like the sauce cook, but it names a late poem by Raymond Carver; the clue's 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carver wrote the poem, and at a Sunday roast the person slicing the meat does the same job.
